explanation: The Aravalli Range is located to the northwest of the Malwa Plateau. It is one of the oldest residual fold mountains in the world, running from Gujarat, through Rajasthan, to Delhi, dividing Rajasthan into northwest and southeast sections.

text: 12. What is the name of the tallest mountain peak of the ancient Aravalli Range, and what is its altitude?

options.text: Guru Shikhar on Mount Abu; 1,722 meters

explanation: The highest peak of the Aravalli Range is Guru Shikhar, located on Mount Abu in the Sirohi district of southwestern Rajasthan, standing at an altitude of 1,722 meters (5,650 feet).

text: 13. The Great Indian Desert, known as the Thar Desert, is located on the western edge of which of the following mountain ranges?
explanation: The Thar Desert is located on the western edge of the Aravalli Range. It is a highly arid region with longitudinal sand dunes and barchans, receiving less than 150 mm of annual rainfall.

text: 14. Which of the following mountain/hill ranges in southern India is world-famous for its massive tea and coffee plantations?
explanation: The Nilgiri Hills, situated at the junction of the Western and Eastern Ghats, are famous for tea and coffee cultivation due to their cool climate, gentle slopes, and acidic, organic-rich soil.

text: 15. Select the correct order of the following plateaus and mountain ranges of India from South to North:

options.text: Malwa Plateau, Satpura Range, Vindhya Range, and Deccan Plateau
Deccan Plateau, Vindhya Range, Satpura Range, and Malwa Plateau
Deccan Plateau, Satpura Range, Vindhya Range, and Malwa Plateau
Malwa Plateau, Vindhya Range, Satpura Range, and Deccan Plateau

explanation: From South to North: Deccan Plateau (South India) -> Satpura Range -> Narmada Valley -> Vindhya Range -> Malwa Plateau (Central/North India).

text: 16. The Vindhyachal mountain range is situated to which geographical direction of the Narmada Rift Valley?
explanation: The Vindhyachal (Vindhya) Range lies to the North of the Narmada Rift Valley, while the Satpura Range lies to its South.

text: 17. The Eastern Ghats are not continuous like the Western Ghats. What is the northernmost starting point and southernmost end point of the Eastern Ghats?

options.text: From the Narmada Valley to the Nilgiri Hills
From the Mahanadi Valley in Odisha to the Nilgiris in the South
From the Tapi Valley to the Cardamom Hills
From the Son Valley to the Vaigai River

explanation: The Eastern Ghats run parallel to the eastern coast of India, stretching from the Mahanadi Valley in Odisha in the north to the Nilgiris in the south, where they meet the Western Ghats.

text: 18. What is the name of the highest mountain peak in the Eastern Ghats, and where is it situated?
explanation: Jindhagada Peak, with an elevation of 1,690 meters located in the Araku Valley of Andhra Pradesh, is the highest peak in the Eastern Ghats. Mahendragiri (1,501 m) is another prominent peak in Odisha.

text: 19. Which of the following mountain peaks is recognized as the highest peak in South India and the Peninsular Plateau overall?
explanation: Anamudi, standing at 2,695 meters (8,842 feet) in the Eravikulam National Park of Idukki district, Kerala, is the highest peak in the Western Ghats, South India, and the Peninsular Plateau.

text: 20. The Western Ghats (Sahyadris) run continuously parallel to the western coast of India. Through how many states do the Western Ghats extend?
explanation: The Western Ghats extend continuously across 6 Indian states: Gujarat, Maharashtra, Goa, Karnataka, Kerala, and Tamil Nadu, spanning approximately 1,600 km.

text: 21. At which of the following mountain nodes do the Eastern Ghats and the Western Ghats meet in southern India?
explanation: The Western Ghats and the Eastern Ghats converge at the Nilgiri Hills (Blue Mountains) in northwestern Tamil Nadu and adjoining parts of Karnataka and Kerala.

text: 22. What is the highest peak of the Nilgiri Hills, which is also the second-highest peak in South India?
explanation: Doda Betta is the highest peak of the Nilgiri Hills, with an elevation of 2,637 meters, serving as a highly visible landmark near Ooty in Tamil Nadu.

text: 23. The Satpura Range is a series of seven folds (block mountains). What is the highest peak of the Satpura Range, and where is it located?

options.text: Dhupgarh near Pachmarhi in Madhya Pradesh

explanation: Mount Dhupgarh is the highest point in the Satpura Range and in the state of Madhya Pradesh, standing at 1,350 meters near the scenic hill station of Pachmarhi.

text: 24. The Amarkantak Plateau, a critical hydrological and geomorphological node of Central India, acts as a radial drainage center for which set of rivers?
explanation: The Amarkantak Plateau is situated at the junction of the Vindhya and Satpura ranges (specifically Maikal Hills). It is the source of the west-flowing Narmada River, north-flowing Son River (tributary of Ganga), and Johilla River, exemplifying radial drainage.

text: 25. Which of the following is the highest peak of the Vindhya Range, also known as 'Goodwill Peak' or 'Kalumar Peak'?
explanation: Sadbhawna Shikhar (also called Goodwill Peak or Kalumar Peak), standing at 752 meters in Damoh district of Madhya Pradesh, is the highest peak of the Vindhya Range.

text: 26. The Chota Nagpur Plateau is a mineral-rich plateau in eastern India. What is its highest mountain peak, which is also an extremely sacred pilgrimage site for Jainism?
explanation: Parasnath Peak, standing at an elevation of 1,365 meters in Giridih district of Jharkhand, is the highest peak of the Chota Nagpur Plateau. It is named after Parsvanatha, the 23rd Tirthankara, and is a major Jain pilgrimage site (Shikharji).

text: 27. In the geomorphology of India, the Meghalaya Plateau (including Garo, Khasi, and Jaintia Hills) is structurally an extension of which of the following physical units?
explanation: The Meghalaya (Shillong) Plateau is structurally an outlier/extension of the Indian Peninsular Plateau. It is separated from the main Chota Nagpur block by a structural depression called the Rajmahal-Garo Gap (Malda Gap).

text: 28. What is the name of the tectonic structural depression that separates the Meghalaya Plateau from the Chota Nagpur / Rajmahal Hills of the Peninsular block?
explanation: The Malda Gap (or Rajmahal-Garo Gap) is a wide, sediment-filled structural depression that separates the Shillong/Meghalaya Plateau from the Rajmahal Hills of Jharkhand.

text: 29. Which of the following passes in the Western Ghats connects Mumbai to Nashik, serving as a vital transport route?
explanation: The Thal Ghat (also called Kasara Ghat) connects Mumbai to Nashik, facilitating rail and road connectivity over the Western Ghats towards northern India.

text: 30. The Bhor Ghat, a prominent mountain pass in the Sahyadri range, connects which two major cities?
explanation: The Bhor Ghat is a major mountain pass that connects Mumbai to Pune, cutting across the Western Ghats to support the Mumbai-Pune Expressway and railway link.

text: 31. The Pal Ghat (Palakkad Gap), a major low-elevation gap breaking the continuity of the Western Ghats, connects which of the following states?
explanation: The Pal Ghat connects Palakkad in Kerala with Coimbatore in Tamil Nadu. It is a vital 30-km-wide gap in the Western Ghats that facilitates trade and climate transmission between the two states.

text: 32. In the physical geography of the Himalayas, what is the term 'Duns' used to define, and where are they primarily found?

options.text: Longitudinal flat-bottomed valleys between the Lesser Himalayas and the Shiwaliks
Sandy desert dunes along the Indus Valley

explanation: Duns are longitudinal, flat-bottomed structural valleys formed between the Lesser Himalayas (Himachal) and the Outer Himalayas (Shiwaliks). Dehradun and Patli Dun are classic examples.

text: 33. Which of the following is the youngest, outermost, and lowest-elevation range of the Himalayas, composed of loose, unconsolidated river sediments?
explanation: The Shiwalik Range represents the southernmost, youngest, and lowest foothills of the Himalayas, formed of loose sandstone, silt, and clay sediments brought down by rivers.

text: 34. The Pir Panjal Range, which is the longest and most prominent mountain range of the Lesser Himalayas, is primarily situated in which state/UT?
explanation: The Pir Panjal Range is a group of inner Himalayan mountains running from Jammu and Kashmir into Himachal Pradesh. It is the longest range of the Lesser Himalayas.

text: 35. In which of the following mountain ranges is the spectacular Zoji La Pass located, connecting Srinagar to Leh?
explanation: The Zoji La Pass is located in the Zaskar Range of Jammu and Kashmir (Ladakh border), serving as a crucial high-altitude link on National Highway 1D between Srinagar and Leh.

text: 36. The highest peak of the Purvachal / Eastern Hills of India is Mount Saramati. In which of the following states is it located?
explanation: Mount Saramati (3,840 meters) is the highest peak of the Purvachal hills, located in the Naga Hills on the international border between Nagaland (India) and Myanmar.

text: 37. In which of the following hill ranges of the Meghalaya Plateau are the wettest places on Earth, Mawsynram and Cherrapunji, situated?
explanation: Mawsynram and Cherrapunji are located on the southern slopes of the East Khasi Hills in Meghalaya. The funnel-shaped orientation of the Khasi Hills traps the moisture-laden monsoon winds from the Bay of Bengal, causing extreme rainfall.

text: 38. The Deccan Plateau of India is characterized by vast sheets of basaltic lava. During which geological period did these extensive volcanic fissure eruptions occur?
explanation: The Deccan Traps (basaltic lava flows) were formed during the late Cretaceous Period (around 66 million years ago) through volcanic fissure eruptions, creating thick layers of basalt rock over a huge area of western and central India.

text: 39. Which of the following soils, also called 'Regur Soil' or 'Black Cotton Soil', is formed due to the weathering of the volcanic basalt rocks of the Deccan Plateau?
explanation: Black soil (Regur) is derived from the weathering of lava/basaltic rocks of the Deccan Traps. It has high clay content, moisture retention capacity, and is highly suitable for cotton cultivation.

text: 40. The Bundelkhand Plateau, located to the north of the Vindhya Range, is famous for its semi-arid terrain and is divided between which of the following states?
explanation: The Bundelkhand region is a hilly and plateau area divided between seven districts of Uttar Pradesh (e.g., Jhansi, Lalitpur) and six districts of Madhya Pradesh.

text: 41. Which of the following mountain passes is located in the state of Sikkim and connects India with the Tibet Autonomous Region of China?
explanation: Nathu La is a mountain pass in the Himalayas, located in Sikkim, connecting it with Tibet. It was closed after the 1962 Sino-Indian War but reopened in 2006 for trade.

text: 42. Which of the following passes connects Himachal Pradesh directly with Tibet and is the point where the Sutlej River enters India?
explanation: Shipki La is a mountain pass and border post on the river Sutlej on the border of India (Himachal Pradesh) and China (Tibet). The Sutlej River cuts through the Greater Himalayas here to enter India.

text: 43. Which mountain pass, located in Jammu and Kashmir, connects Jammu with Srinagar across the Pir Panjal Range and houses the famous Jawahar Tunnel?
explanation: Banihal Pass (elevation 2,832 m) connects the Kashmir Valley to the outer Himalayas and southern plains. The historic Jawahar Tunnel, constructed in 1956, facilitates year-round road connectivity.

text: 44. The strategically important Bom Di La pass, which connects Lhasa (Tibet) with the western plains of Assam, is situated in which Indian state?
explanation: Bom Di La pass is situated in the western part of Arunachal Pradesh, connecting the Kameng district to Lhasa, Tibet.

text: 45. Which of the following passes connects the Lahul valley of Himachal Pradesh with Ladakh and serves as the water divide between the Bhaga and Chandra rivers?
explanation: Bara Lacha La (4,890 m) is a high mountain pass in the Zaskar Range connecting Lahaul district in Himachal Pradesh to Leh district in Ladakh.

text: 46. Which pass located in the state of Uttarakhand serves as a major route for the sacred Kailash-Manasarovar Pilgrimage?
explanation: Lipulekh Pass is located on the tri-junction of Uttarakhand (India), Tibet (China), and Nepal. It is actively used by pilgrims traveling to Mount Kailash and Lake Manasarovar.

text: 47. In which of the following mountain ranges is the Khardung La pass, historically celebrated as one of the highest motorable passes in the world, situated?
explanation: Khardung La is situated in the Ladakh Range, north of Leh. It connects the Indus River Valley to the Shyok and Nubra Valleys.

text: 48. The Rohtang Pass, a highly visited tourist destination cutting across the Pir Panjal Range, connects which two valleys of Himachal Pradesh?
explanation: Rohtang Pass (3,978 m) connects the Kullu Valley with the high-altitude, semi-arid Lahaul and Spiti Valleys of Himachal Pradesh.

text: 49. Which of the following hill ranges represents the southern portion of the Eastern Ghats, situated in the state of Tamil Nadu?
explanation: The Shevaroy Hills are located in the Salem district of Tamil Nadu. Along with the Javadi Hills, they form the southernmost extensions of the Eastern Ghats.

text: 50. The Javadi Hills, a highly dissected group of hills on the Eastern Ghats, are primarily located in which state?
explanation: The Javadi Hills are an extension of the Eastern Ghats spread across parts of Vellore and Tiruvannamalai districts in northern Tamil Nadu.

text: 51. Which of the following hill ranges is situated in Andhra Pradesh and forms a part of the Eastern Ghats, located between the Krishna and Pennar rivers?
explanation: The Nallamala Hills are located in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana. They run parallel to the Coromandel Coast and form a significant part of the Eastern Ghats.

text: 52. The Baba Budan Giri Hills, famous for being the site of the earliest coffee plantations in India during the 17th century, are located in which state?
explanation: Baba Budan Giri is a mountain range in the Western Ghats (Chhikmagalur district) of Karnataka. It is historically famous for the introduction of coffee crops by Sufi saint Baba Budan.

text: 53. The Mikir Hills, which represent a rugged terrain of crystalline rocks, are located in which of the following states?
explanation: The Mikir Hills are a group of hills located to the south of the Kaziranga National Park in Assam. They are structurally part of the Karbi-Meghalaya Plateau outlier.

text: 54. The Abor, Mishmi, and Dafla Hills represent outer foothills of the Himalayas. In which state are they situated?
explanation: The Dafla, Miri, Abor, and Mishmi Hills are situated in Arunachal Pradesh, named after the native tribes that inhabit these northern outermost tracts of the Himalayas.

text: 55. Which hill range represents the southernmost hill tract of the Western Ghats, famous for cardamoms, pepper, and coffee?
explanation: The Cardamom Hills (Yela Mala) are located in Kerala and Tamil Nadu. They represent the southern tip of the Western Ghats, highly suitable for cash crops.

text: 56. The Palani Hills, an eastward extension of the Western Ghats, are entirely located within which of the following states?
explanation: The Palani Hills are situated mostly in the Dindigul district of Tamil Nadu. The famous hill station of Kodaikanal is located in this range.

text: 57. In the glaciology of the Trans-Himalayas, the Baltoro Glacier is one of the longest non-polar valley glaciers. In which range is it situated?
explanation: The Baltoro Glacier is located in the Karakoram Range of Gilgit-Baltistan. It is 63 km long and feeds the Shigar River.

text: 58. Apart from Siachen and Baltoro, the Biafo and Hispar glaciers are massive glacial units. In which of the following regions are they located?
explanation: Both the Biafo (67 km long) and Hispar (49 km long) glaciers are situated in the Karakoram Range, forming the world's longest continuous glacial highway outside the polar regions.

text: 59. The Kathiawar Peninsula, characterized by the Gir Range and radial drainage, is located in which of the following states?
explanation: The Kathiawar Peninsula represents a distinct landmass of Gujarat, bounded by the Gulf of Kutch to the north-west and the Gulf of Khambhat to the east.

text: 60. The Dandakaranya region, structurally a part of the Peninsular Plateau, is spread across which of the following sets of states?
explanation: Dandakaranya is a historical and geographical region of India, covering a vast area of Bastar (Chhattisgarh), Koraput (Odisha), and parts of Andhra Pradesh.

text: 61. In the regional geography of the Karnataka Plateau, what are the local geomorphological terms used to distinguish the hilly, forested tracts from the undulating plains?
explanation: In Karnataka, the highly dissected Western Ghats upland is called 'Malnad' (hilly country), while the flatter, open undulating plains to the east are called 'Maidan'.

text: 62. Which of the following plateaus is a basaltic tableland located between the Aravalli Range and the Vindhya Range, drained by the Chambal River?
explanation: The Malwa Plateau is situated in western Madhya Pradesh and parts of Rajasthan. It is a volcanic plateau drained by the Chambal River and its tributaries (Kali Sindh, Parbati, Betwa).

text: 63. The Zaskar Range, a major mountain range of the Trans-Himalayas, lies to the south of which river valley?
explanation: The Zaskar Range lies parallel and to the south of the Indus River Valley. The Ladakh Range lies parallel and to the north of the Indus River.

text: 64. The Kumaon Himalayas are famous for hosting several beautiful lakes. In which state is this physical division located?
explanation: The Kumaon Himalayas lie entirely within the state of Uttarakhand, bounded by the Satluj River on the west and the Kali River on the east.

text: 65. In which of the following mountain passes is the historic Jawahar Tunnel, designed for all-weather connectivity, situated?
explanation: The Jawahar Tunnel (or Banihal Tunnel) was constructed beneath the Banihal Pass in 1956 to ensure year-round road transport between Jammu and Srinagar.

text: 66. Which high-altitude mountain pass connects Ladakh to Tibet and was historically part of the southern silk route?
explanation: Lanak La is a high mountain pass in the Aksai Chin region of eastern Ladakh, traditionally serving as the border/route connecting Ladakh to Tibet.

text: 67. The Jelep La pass, which is a vital link between Kalimpong (West Bengal) and Lhasa (Tibet), is located in which state?
explanation: Jelep La pass (4,267 m) is located in East Sikkim. It is close to Nathu La and connects Kalimpong in West Bengal directly to Lhasa.

text: 68. Which of the following is the highest peak of the state of Maharashtra, located in the Western Ghats (Sahyadris)?
explanation: Kalsubai Peak, standing at an elevation of 1,646 meters (5,400 ft) in Ahmednagar district, is the highest point/peak in Maharashtra.

text: 69. Kudremukh, a prominent mountain peak in the Western Ghats famous for its iron ore deposits, is located in which state?
explanation: Kudremukh is a peak in Chikkamagaluru district of Karnataka, shaped like a horse's face (Kudre = Horse, Mukh = Face). It was famous for iron-ore mining.

text: 70. Mullayanagiri is currently recorded as the highest peak of which of the following Indian states?
explanation: Mullayanagiri, with an elevation of 1,930 meters in the Baba Budan Giri Range, is the highest mountain peak in the state of Karnataka.

text: 71. Which of the following passes in the Western Ghats connects Madurai in Tamil Nadu with Kollam in Kerala, acting as a crucial transport gap south of the Palghat Gap?
explanation: The Shencottah Gap is an important pass in the Western Ghats that connects the city of Madurai in Tamil Nadu with Kollam in Kerala. It is located just south of the Cardamom Hills.

text: 72. Which of the following mountain passes is located in the state of Arunachal Pradesh, connects Tawang with the rest of India, and remains snow-covered during most of the winter?
explanation: Sela Pass is a high-altitude mountain pass located in the Tawang district of Arunachal Pradesh. It stands at an elevation of 4,170 meters and is of great strategic importance for national security.

text: 73. The Pangsau Pass, which provides a major land transport route across the Patkai Hills between India and Myanmar, is situated on the border of Myanmar and which Indian state?
explanation: Pangsau Pass lies on the crest of the Patkai Range on the India-Myanmar border, connecting the Changlang district of Arunachal Pradesh with Myanmar. It is famous for the historic 'Stillwell Road' built during World War II.

text: 74. Which of the following mountain passes is situated on the tri-junction of India (Arunachal Pradesh), China, and Myanmar, and is a major disputed border point?
explanation: Diphu Pass is located on the tri-point border of India, China, and Myanmar in eastern Arunachal Pradesh. It lies on the strategic McMahon Line and remains a key point of geopolitical interest.

text: 75. The Mana Pass and Niti Pass, which have been historically used for trade between India and Tibet, are situated in which of the following states?
explanation: Both Mana Pass (5,545 meters) and Niti Pass are situated in the Garhwal region of Uttarakhand, connecting India with Tibet. Mana Pass is located near the holy town of Badrinath.

text: 76. The Debsa Pass, a high-altitude mountain pass in the Greater Himalayas that connects the Kullu and Spiti valleys, is located in which state?
explanation: Debsa Pass is a 5,360-meter-high mountain pass located in the Greater Himalayas of Himachal Pradesh, connecting the Parvati Valley of Kullu with the Spiti Valley.

text: 77. Gangotri Glacier, the massive glacial ice body and the source of the Bhagirathi River (the main stream of Ganga), is situated in which of the following mountain ranges?
explanation: Gangotri Glacier is situated in the Uttarkashi district of Uttarakhand, in the Kumaon-Garhwal division of the Greater Himalayas. The snout of the glacier is known as Gaumukh, from which Bhagirathi River originates.

text: 78. The Yamunotri Glacier, the source of the sacred Yamuna River, is located on the southern slopes of which of the following prominent Himalayan peaks?
explanation: Yamunotri Glacier lies in Uttarakhand on the bandarpunch (Bunderpunch) massif of the Greater Himalayas at an elevation of about 6,387 meters, feeding the Yamuna River.

text: 79. The Milam Glacier, which is the primary source of the Goriganga River, is a major glacier of which physical division of the Himalayas?
explanation: The Milam Glacier is located in the Pithoragarh district of Uttarakhand, in the Kumaon Himalayas. It is a major source of the Goriganga River, which later merges with the Kali River.

text: 80. The Karbi Anglong Plateau, structurally a fractured block of the ancient Indian shield, is located in which state of Northeast India?
explanation: The Karbi Anglong Plateau is located in Assam. Structurally, it is an extension of the Peninsular Indian Shield (Karbi-Meghalaya Plateau outlier), separated from the main Deccan block by the Malda Gap.

text: 81. The Pachaimalai Hills and Sirumalai Hills are prominent, deeply dissected hill ranges belonging to the Eastern Ghats. In which of the following states are they situated?
explanation: Both Pachaimalai (Green Hills) and Sirumalai hill ranges are located in Tamil Nadu, forming dissected, isolated residual parts of the Eastern Ghats.

text: 82. The Varushanad Hills, which house the highly scenic Megamalai Wildlife Sanctuary, represent a southern hill range of which physical division of India?
explanation: The Varushanad Hills are an eastward-extending spur of the Western Ghats in southern Tamil Nadu, bordering Kerala. They lie south of the Palani Hills and house the headwaters of the Vaigai River.

text: 83. The Baghelkhand Plateau, which is characterized by Gondwana rock formations and rich coal deposits, lies east of the Maikal Range and is divided between which states?
explanation: The Baghelkhand Plateau is located in central India, covering the northeastern part of Madhya Pradesh and the northern part of Chhattisgarh. It is famous for its sandstone and coal beds.

text: 84. The Kutch Peninsula in Gujarat is structurally separated from the Kathiawar Peninsula by which of the following geographic features?
explanation: The Gulf of Kutch is a water inlet of the Arabian Sea that separates the arid Kutch Peninsula (to the north) from the Kathiawar Peninsula (to the south) in Gujarat.

text: 85. With an elevation of 7,816 meters, Nanda Devi holds what unique status among the highest mountain peaks in India?

options.text: It is the second-highest peak in the Karakoram range.
It is the highest mountain peak situated entirely within the sovereign territory of India.
It is the oldest volcanic peak in the world.
It is situated on the international border of India and Myanmar.

explanation: Mount Nanda Devi is the highest mountain peak situated entirely within the sovereign boundaries of India (since K2 is in POK and Kanchenjunga is on the border of Sikkim and Nepal). It is located in Chamoli district of Uttarakhand.

text: 86. Kamet Peak (7,756 meters) and Trishul Peak (7,120 meters) are major mountain massifs situated in which regional division of the Indian Himalayas?
explanation: Kamet and Trishul are major peaks of the Garhwal-Kumaon Himalayas, situated in the state of Uttarakhand. They represent prominent snow-capped summits of the Greater Himalayan range.

text: 87. The Chogo Lungma and Hispar glaciers, which are major sources of river waters in the Karakoram region, are located in which political/geographical territory?
explanation: The Chogo Lungma and Hispar glaciers are massive valley glaciers located in the Karakoram Range of Gilgit-Baltistan. They are vital hydrological networks for the upper Indus basin.

text: 88. In the structural geology of the Indian shield, which gap represents a major tectonic fault zone separating the Eastern Ghats from the Nilgiri hills?
explanation: The Moyar Gorge (or Moyar Trench) is a deep, steep tectonic gorge that separates the Nilgiri Plateau on the south from the Biligirirangana Hills and Karnataka Plateau on the north, acting as the structural boundary between Eastern and Western Ghats.

text: 89. The Bastar Plateau, which constitutes the southern portion of Chhattisgarh and is famous for its rich mineral deposits (especially tin ore), is structurally part of which larger plateau?
explanation: The Bastar Plateau forms a core part of the Dandakaranya region of India, structurally composed of Archean granites and gneisses, rich in iron ore, tin, and bauxite.

text: 90. The Rohtang Pass has been bypassed by which of the following engineering marvels, providing all-weather connectivity to the Lahaul-Spiti valley?
explanation: The Atal Tunnel, constructed at an altitude of over 3,000 meters under the Rohtang Pass in Himachal Pradesh, is the longest highway single-tube tunnel above 10,000 feet, connecting Manali to Lahaul-Spiti valley.

text: 91. The Haldighat Pass, historically famous for the Battle of Haldighati (1576) between Akbar's forces and Maharana Pratap, is located in which mountain range?
explanation: The Haldighat Pass is a mountain pass in the Aravalli Range of Rajasthan, connecting Rajsamand and Pali districts. It is named after its turmeric-colored yellow soil (Haldi = Turmeric, Ghat = Pass).

text: 92. The Pindari Glacier, which is located in the upper reaches of the Kumaon Himalayas, is famous for giving rise to which tributary of the Alaknanda River?
explanation: The Pindari Glacier in the Bageshwar district of Uttarakhand gives rise to the Pindar River, which flows southwest to merge with the Alaknanda River at Karnaprayag.

text: 93. The Sela Pass in Arunachal Pradesh is located at an altitude of approximately 4,170 meters. Which two major strategic military outposts does it lie between?
explanation: Sela Pass is situated between Tezpur (Assam) and Tawang (Arunachal Pradesh), serving as the sole roadway connection to the strategic Tawang sector near the India-China border.

text: 94. The Satpura Range consists of several prominent hill ranges from west to east. Which of the following is the correct order of these hills from west to east?

options.text: Rajpipla Hills, Mahadeo Hills, and Maikal Hills
Maikal Hills, Mahadeo Hills, and Rajpipla Hills
Mahadeo Hills, Rajpipla Hills, and Maikal Hills
Rajpipla Hills, Maikal Hills, and Mahadeo Hills

explanation: The Satpura Range is divided into three distinct segments from west to east: the Rajpipla Hills (westernmost), the Mahadeo Hills (central, housing Pachmarhi and Dhupgarh), and the Maikal Hills (easternmost, containing Amarkantak).

text: 95. Mount Abu, which houses the highest peak of the Aravalli Range (Guru Shikhar), is structurally classified as what type of physical feature?
explanation: Mount Abu is an isolated rocky plateau in the Aravalli Range, rising abruptly as a steep granite block mountain (inselberg/horst) surrounded by flatter plains.

text: 96. Which of the following waterfalls in India, falling from a height of 310 meters on the Mandovi River, is famously called the 'Sea of Milk'?
explanation: Dudhsagar Falls is located on the Mandovi River along the border of Goa and Karnataka. The waterfall plunges from a height of 310 meters (1017 feet) and its name literally means 'Sea of Milk'.

text: 97. The Kunchikal Falls, recognized as the highest waterfall in India (455 meters), are formed by the Varahi River in which district of Karnataka?
explanation: Kunchikal Falls are formed by the Varahi River near Masthikatte-Yadur in the Shimoga (Shivamogga) district of Karnataka. They stand at a total height of 455 meters, making them the tallest in India.

text: 98. The Pachaimalai Hills of the Eastern Ghats derive their name from the Tamil word 'Pachai'. What does this name literally translate to in English, representing the local landscape?
explanation: The word 'Pachai' in Tamil means 'Green'. The Pachaimalai Hills are famous for their lush, green vegetation and micro-climatic moist forests relative to the surrounding dry plains.

text: 99. In the regional geomorphology of Jammu & Kashmir, the Pir Panjal Range is structurally separated from the Great Himalayan Range by which of the following tectonic features?

options.text: The Kashmir Valley (a structural synclinal basin)

explanation: The beautiful Kashmir Valley is a major structural synclinal basin (oval valley) lying between the Pir Panjal Range (on the southwest) and the Great Himalayan Zaskar Range (on the northeast).

text: 100. The highest peak of the Purvachal Range, Mount Saramati (3,840 meters), is located on the international border of India and which neighboring country?
explanation: Mount Saramati is the highest peak in Nagaland and the Purvachal hills. It is situated on the international border between Nagaland (India) and Myanmar (Sagaing Region).

text: 1. Which of the following cosmic theories, first proposed by Georges Lemaître in 1927, is widely accepted as the explanation for the origin and expansion of our Universe?
explanation: The Big Bang Theory, first proposed by Belgian priest and astronomer Georges Lemaître, posits that the universe expanded from an extremely hot and dense single point (singularity) approximately 13.8 billion years ago.

text: 2. In our Solar System, which of the following natural satellites holds the distinction of being the largest moon, even surpassing the planet Mercury in physical size?
explanation: Ganymede, a satellite of Jupiter, is the largest moon in the Solar System. It has a diameter of 5,268 km, which is larger than the planet Mercury (4,879 km) and the dwarf planet Pluto.

text: 3. Most planets in our solar system rotate on their axes in an anti-clockwise direction (West to East). Which of the following planets exhibits retrograde (clockwise) rotation?
explanation: Venus and Uranus are the only two planets in our Solar System that rotate from East to West (clockwise or retrograde rotation). All other planets rotate from West to East (anti-clockwise).

text: 4. Despite Mercury being the closest planet to the Sun, Venus is recorded as the hottest planet in our Solar System. What is the primary atmospheric reason for this?

options.text: High concentration of active volcanoes on its surface
An extremely dense atmosphere composed of 96% carbon dioxide ($CO_2$), trapping solar heat
Its proximity to the asteroid belt releasing thermal radiation
The lack of any natural satellite allowing uninterrupted solar wind absorption

explanation: Venus's thick, dense atmosphere is composed mostly of Carbon Dioxide ($CO_2$), along with clouds of sulfuric acid. This creates a runaway greenhouse effect that traps solar heat, raising surface temperatures to about 465°C.

text: 5. In the planetary architecture of our solar system, the Asteroid Belt is situated in the vast gap between the orbits of which two planets?
explanation: The Asteroid Belt is a torus-shaped region located in the space between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter. It contains millions of irregular rock bodies called asteroids or minor planets.

text: 6. Halley's Comet, a famous periodic comet that is visible from Earth with the naked eye, has an orbital period of approximately how many years?
explanation: Halley's Comet is a periodic comet with an orbital period of about 75-76 years. It was last seen in the inner Solar System in 1986 and is projected to return in mid-2061.

text: 7. To determine the absolute age of the Earth and its oldest rock samples, which of the following physical-chemical techniques is primarily utilized?

options.text: Radioactive dating using Uranium-Lead / Lead-Lead decay series

explanation: Uranium-lead and lead-lead radioactive dating are used to calculate the age of the Earth (estimated at 4.54 billion years) because their isotopes have extremely long half-lives. Carbon-14 dating has a short half-life (~5,730 years) and is only useful for organic material under 50,000 years old.

text: 8. In physical geography, the precise shape of the Earth is not a perfect sphere but is classified as which of the following geometric structures?
explanation: The Earth is an oblate spheroid or geoid. Due to its rotation on its axis, centrifugal force causes the Earth to bulge slightly at the Equator and flatten at the poles.

text: 9. Earth's axis of rotation is tilted relative to its orbital plane. What is the angle of this axial tilt relative to the perpendicular to the orbital plane, and what angle does the axis make with the orbital plane itself?

options.text: 23.5° with the perpendicular; 66.5° with the orbital plane
66.5° with the perpendicular; 23.5° with the orbital plane
45.0° with the perpendicular; 45.0° with the orbital plane
90.0° with the perpendicular; 0.0° with the orbital plane

explanation: The Earth's axis of rotation is tilted at an angle of 23.5° relative to the perpendicular (normal) to its orbital plane. Consequently, the axis makes an angle of 66.5° (90° - 23.5°) with the orbital plane itself.

text: 10. The rotation of the Earth on its axis from West to East produces several major physical consequences. Which of the following is NOT a consequence of Earth's rotation?

options.text: The occurrence of day and night
The deflection of winds and ocean currents due to the Coriolis Force
The rise and fall of daily tides

explanation: The change of seasons is a consequence of the Earth's revolution around the Sun in combination with its tilted axis. Rotation on its axis causes day/night, the Coriolis deflection, and daily tidal cycles.

text: 11. The Coriolis effect, caused by the Earth's rapid rotation, deflects moving air and water. According to Ferrel's Law, in which directions are they deflected in the Northern and Southern Hemispheres respectively?

options.text: To the left in the Northern Hemisphere; to the right in the Southern Hemisphere
To the right in the Northern Hemisphere; to the left in the Southern Hemisphere

explanation: Coriolis force deflects moving objects (winds/currents) to the right of their path of motion in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left of their path of motion in the Southern Hemisphere.

text: 12. What are the two primary mechanical factors that together cause the change of seasons and the varying lengths of day and night on Earth?

options.text: Earth's rotation and its distance from the moon
Earth's revolution around the Sun and the constant tilt of its axis
Fluctuations in solar radiation and volcanic dust
Precession of the equinoxes and magnetic reversals

explanation: The change of seasons and the varying duration of day and night are caused by the Earth's annual revolution around the Sun and the fixed tilt of the Earth's axis of rotation (parallelism of the axis).

text: 13. In its elliptical orbit, the Earth is closest to the Sun at a point called 'Perihelion'. On approximately what date does this occur, and what is the distance?
explanation: At Perihelion, the Earth is at its closest distance to the Sun (approximately 147 million km). This occurs annually around January 3.

text: 14. The point in Earth's elliptical orbit where it is farthest from the Sun is called 'Aphelion'. On approximately what date does this occur, and what is the distance?
explanation: At Aphelion, the Earth is at its farthest distance from the Sun (approximately 152 million km). This occurs annually around July 4.

text: 15. The Summer Solstice represents the day with the longest duration of daylight in the Northern Hemisphere. On which of the following dates does it typically fall?
explanation: On June 21, the Northern Hemisphere is tilted maximum towards the Sun, and the Sun's rays fall vertically on the Tropic of Cancer ($23.5^\circ$N), resulting in the longest day of the year in the Northern Hemisphere (Summer Solstice).

text: 16. The Winter Solstice marks the shortest day and longest night of the year in the Northern Hemisphere. On which date does this occur?
explanation: On December 22, the Southern Hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun, and the Sun's rays fall vertically on the Tropic of Capricorn ($23.5^\circ$S). This is the Winter Solstice in the Northern Hemisphere, marking its shortest day.

text: 17. Twice a year, the Sun's rays fall vertically over the Earth's Equator, resulting in equal day and night durations of 12 hours across the globe. What are these dates called, and when do they occur?

options.text: Aphelion and Perihelion; January 3 and July 4

explanation: Equinoxes occur on March 21 (Vernal/Spring Equinox) and September 23 (Autumnal Equinox) when the Sun is directly above the Equator. On these dates, day and night are of equal length globally.

text: 18. The phenomenon of the 'Midnight Sun', where the Sun does not set below the horizon for several weeks, is experienced in which of the following zones?

options.text: Polar and Sub-polar regions beyond the Arctic and Antarctic Circles

explanation: The Midnight Sun occurs during the summer months in regions north of the Arctic Circle and south of the Antarctic Circle due to Earth's axial tilt keeping these polar regions facing the Sun even as the Earth rotates.

text: 19. Which of the following statements is true regarding lines of Latitude (parallels) on Earth?

options.text: They all intersect at the North and South Poles.
They are of equal length around the globe.
They are parallel circles, and the distance between any two degrees of latitude is approximately 111 km.
They are used to determine local timezone boundaries.

explanation: Latitudes run parallel to the Equator and never intersect. The linear distance between each degree of latitude is approximately constant at 111 kilometers (69 miles).

text: 20. Unlike latitudes, lines of Longitude (meridians) exhibit different spatial properties. Which of the following is a key characteristic of longitudes?

options.text: They are parallel to each other and never meet.
They converge and meet at the North and South Poles, with their maximum distance apart at the Equator.
They are used to define the boundaries of different climatic zones.
They decrease in length as they move towards the poles.

explanation: Longitudes are semi-circles that run from pole to pole and converge at the North and South Poles. Because they converge, the distance between longitudes is maximum at the Equator (~111.3 km) and decreases to zero at the poles.

text: 21. By international agreement, the Prime Meridian is defined as the meridian of $0^\circ$ longitude. Near which of the following cities does this meridian pass?
explanation: The Prime Meridian ($0^\circ$ longitude) passes through the Royal Observatory at Greenwich, near London, UK. It is the starting point for measuring longitude east and west around the globe.

text: 22. The International Date Line (IDL) lies on approximately $180^\circ$ longitude. Which of the following is true when a traveler crosses the IDL from East to West (from America to Asia)?

options.text: They gain (add) 24 hours (advance a full day).
No time change occurs because the line is in the ocean.
They gain exactly 5 hours and 30 minutes.

explanation: When crossing the International Date Line from East to West (e.g., from San Francisco to Tokyo), travelers cross into a later calendar day, meaning they gain/advance 1 day. Crossing from West to East (Asia to America) causes them to repeat/lose a day.

text: 23. Why does the International Date Line deviate (zigzag) from the straight meridian of $180^\circ$ longitude at several places?

options.text: To align with the magnetic poles of the Earth
To prevent dividing a single country or island group into two different calendar days
To account for the oceanic rift valley topography
To avoid entering the territorial waters of Russia

explanation: The IDL is bent or zigzagged at several places (e.g., Aleutian Islands, Fiji, Kiribati) to avoid dividing political territories, landmasses, or island nations into two different calendar dates, ensuring administrative uniformity.

text: 24. Since the Earth rotates $360^\circ$ in 24 hours ($15^\circ$ in 1 hour), time changes with longitude. If it is 12:00 Noon at the Prime Meridian (GMT), what is the local standard time at the Indian Standard Meridian ($82^\circ30'E$)?
explanation: Since India is East of Greenwich, its time is ahead. Calculation: $82.5^\circ \times 4$ minutes/degree = $330$ minutes = 5 hours and 30 minutes. Thus, standard time in India is GMT + 5:30, which equals 5:30 PM.

text: 25. If the local time at place X ($15^\circ$W longitude) is 10:00 AM on a Tuesday, what will be the local time at place Y ($45^\circ$E longitude)?
explanation: Total longitude difference between $15^\circ$W and $45^\circ$E is $15 + 45 = 60^\circ$. Since $15^\circ = 1$ hour, $60^\circ$ corresponds to a 4-hour difference. Since place Y is further East, we add 4 hours to X's time (10:00 AM + 4 hours = 2:00 PM Tuesday).

text: 26. The Indian Standard Time (IST) meridian of $82^\circ30'E$ passes through five Indian states. Which of the following is NOT one of these five states?
explanation: The standard meridian of India ($82^\circ30'E$) passes through five states: Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Odisha, and Andhra Pradesh. It does not pass through Jharkhand.

text: 27. A Solar Eclipse occurs when the Moon blocks the light of the Sun from reaching Earth. Which of the following astronomical alignments is correct for a solar eclipse to occur?

options.text: Sun - Earth - Moon, occurring during a Full Moon
Sun - Moon - Earth, occurring during a New Moon
Moon - Sun - Earth, occurring during an Equinox
Earth - Sun - Moon, occurring during a Solstice

explanation: A Solar Eclipse occurs during a New Moon (Amavasya) when the Moon is directly between the Sun and the Earth (Sun - Moon - Earth alignment), casting its shadow on the Earth.

text: 28. A Lunar Eclipse occurs when the Earth casts its shadow on the Moon. Which alignment and moon phase are required for a lunar eclipse?

options.text: Sun - Moon - Earth, during a New Moon
Sun - Earth - Moon, during a Full Moon
Earth - Moon - Sun, during a Crescent Moon
Sun - Earth - Moon, during a Half Moon

explanation: A Lunar Eclipse occurs during a Full Moon (Purnima) when the Earth is positioned directly between the Sun and the Moon (Sun - Earth - Moon alignment), blocking solar light from reaching the Moon.

text: 29. During which moon phases do 'Spring Tides' (extremely high high-tides and low low-tides) occur, and what is the physical cause?

options.text: Quarter Moons; when the Sun and Moon are at $90^\circ$ angles relative to Earth
New Moon and Full Moon; when the Sun, Moon, and Earth are in a straight line (Syzygy)
Equinoxes; when the Sun is directly over the Equator
Solstices; when the Earth is at its maximum tilt

explanation: Spring Tides occur during the New Moon and Full Moon when the gravitational pulls of the Sun and the Moon act along the same line (Syzygy/Conjunction), reinforcing each other to produce maximum tidal ranges.

text: 30. 'Neap Tides', which exhibit a much smaller tidal range, occur during which of the following moon phases?
explanation: Neap Tides occur during the first and third quarter moons when the Sun and Moon are at right angles ($90^\circ$ or quadrature) relative to the Earth, causing their gravitational pulls to oppose and partially cancel each other out.

text: 31. Why is the same side of the Moon always visible to us from the Earth?

options.text: The Moon does not rotate on its axis at all.
The Moon has a synchronous rotation, where its rotation period on its axis is equal to its revolution period around the Earth.
The Earth's gravity prevents the backside of the Moon from turning.
The reflection of sunlight is blocked on the far side of the Moon.

explanation: The Moon exhibits synchronous rotation (or tidal locking) because it takes the exact same time (approximately 27.3 days) to rotate once on its axis as it does to complete one orbit around the Earth.

text: 32. In lunar mechanics, what is the term used to describe the point in the Moon's elliptical orbit where it is closest to the Earth?
explanation: Perigee is the point in the Moon's orbit where it is closest to the Earth, making the Moon appear larger in the sky (Supermoon). Apogee is the point where the Moon is farthest from the Earth.

text: 33. In astrophysics and stellar geography, what physical quantity does a 'Light-Year' measure?
explanation: A Light-Year is a unit of astronomical distance. It is defined as the total distance that light travels in a vacuum in one Earth year, equivalent to about 9.46 trillion kilometers.

text: 34. What is an Astronomical Unit (AU) technically defined as?

options.text: The distance traveled by light in one second
The mean distance between the center of the Earth and the center of the Sun
The distance between the Sun and its closest neighboring star
The radius of our Milky Way Galaxy

explanation: An Astronomical Unit (AU) is a unit of length used in astronomy, equal to the mean distance from the Earth to the Sun (approximately 149.6 million kilometers or 93 million miles).

text: 35. Which of the gas giant planets in our Solar System has the lowest bulk density, so much so that it is less dense than liquid water?
explanation: Saturn has the lowest average density of all planets in our Solar System (about 0.697 g/cm³), which is less than the density of water (1.0 g/cm³). Thus, Saturn would theoretically float in a massive tub of water.

text: 36. In astrobiology, what is the 'Goldilocks Zone' (or Habitable Zone) defined as?

options.text: The central core of a star where active fusion occurs
The region around a star where orbital velocities are perfectly stable
The range of distance from a host star where planetary temperatures allow liquid water to exist on its surface
The outer ring of a galaxy containing high cosmic dust

explanation: The Goldilocks Zone represents the habitable zone around a star where conditions are 'just right' (neither too hot nor too cold) for liquid water to exist on the surface of an orbiting planet, which is vital for life.

text: 37. According to Kepler's First Law of Planetary Motion, planets move around the Sun in what shape of orbit, and where is the Sun positioned?

options.text: Circular orbit with the Sun at the center
Elliptical orbit with the Sun at one of the two foci
Parabolic orbit with the Sun shifting continuously
Perfect helical path with the Sun at the apex

explanation: Kepler's First Law (Law of Ellipses) states that all planets orbit the Sun in elliptical paths, with the Sun situated at one of the two focal points (foci) of the ellipse.

text: 38. Which of the following planets has the highest average density in our entire Solar System?
explanation: Earth is the densest planet in the Solar System, with an average density of approximately 5.515 g/cm³. Mercury is the second densest (5.427 g/cm³).

text: 39. What are the exact latitudinal positions of the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn on Earth?
explanation: The Tropic of Cancer is situated at $23^\circ30'$N (or $23.5^\circ$N) in the Northern Hemisphere, and the Tropic of Capricorn is situated at $23^\circ30'$S (or $23.5^\circ$S) in the Southern Hemisphere.

text: 40. The Tropic of Cancer ($23.5^\circ$N) passes through how many Indian states?
explanation: The Tropic of Cancer passes through 8 Indian states: Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura, and Mizoram.

text: 41. Which of the following layers of the Sun's atmosphere is visible to the naked eye during a total solar eclipse as a glowing, halo-like outer crown?
explanation: The Corona is the outermost layer of the Sun's atmosphere, extending millions of kilometers into space. It is extremely hot but faint, becoming visible as a spectacular white crown of light only during a total solar eclipse when the bright Photosphere is completely blocked.

text: 42. The visible surface of the Sun from which light is continuously emitted into space is known as which of the following layers?
explanation: The Photosphere is the deeply bright, visible surface layer of the Sun. It has an average temperature of about 5,500°C to 6,000°C and is the region from which sunspots emerge.

text: 43. The periodic rise and fall in the number of sunspots on the Sun's surface, which significantly impacts space weather and geomagnetic activity, follows a cycle of approximately how many years?
explanation: The Sunspot Cycle (or Solar Magnetic Activity Cycle) has a duration of approximately 11 years. During this cycle, the Sun's magnetic poles flip, and solar activity transitions between solar minimum and solar maximum.

text: 44. The spectacular glowing light displays in Earth's high-latitude regions, known as auroras, are caused by the collision of charged solar wind particles with atmospheric gases. What are these auroras called in the Northern and Southern Hemispheres respectively?
explanation: In the Northern Hemisphere, the display is called the Aurora Borealis (Northern Lights). In the Southern Hemisphere, it is called the Aurora Australis (Southern Lights). They occur when solar winds collide with oxygen and nitrogen molecules in the thermosphere, guided by Earth's magnetic field lines.

text: 45. To escape Earth's gravitational pull and enter space without falling back, what is the minimum initial velocity (escape velocity) required for a projectile launched from Earth's surface?
explanation: The escape velocity of Earth is approximately 11.2 km/s (about 40,270 km/h). This is the speed needed for an unpowered object to break free from Earth's gravitational influence.

text: 46. Because of its smaller mass and weaker gravity, what is the approximate escape velocity of the Moon, explaining why it cannot retain a permanent atmosphere?
explanation: The Moon has an escape velocity of approximately 2.38 km/s. Because this speed is so low, gas molecules easily exceed it due to solar heating, causing them to escape into space and preventing the formation of an atmosphere.

text: 47. In climatology and planetary physics, the term 'Albedo' refers to which of the following mechanical properties?

options.text: The amount of solar energy absorbed by a planet's core
The fraction of solar radiation reflected back into space from a celestial body's surface and atmosphere
The speed at which a planet radiates thermal energy
The density of greenhouse gases in a planetary atmosphere

explanation: Albedo is a measure of the reflectivity of a surface. It is expressed as a decimal or percentage from 0 (perfect absorber) to 1 (perfect reflector). Earth's average albedo is about 0.30 (or 30%).

text: 48. Which of the following surfaces on Earth possesses the highest albedo, reflecting the maximum percentage of incoming solar radiation?
explanation: Fresh snow and ice have the highest albedo on Earth, reflecting up to 80% to 90% of incoming sunlight. Oceans have a very low albedo (reflecting only ~6%), absorbing most solar heat.

text: 49. Kepler's Second Law of Planetary Motion, also known as the Law of Equal Areas, has what physical implication for a planet's orbital speed as it moves around the Sun?

options.text: The planet moves at a constant speed throughout its orbit.
The planet moves fastest when it is closest to the Sun (Perihelion) and slowest when it is farthest (Aphelion).
The planet moves slowest when it is closest to the Sun and fastest when it is farthest.
The planet's speed decreases exponentially over geological time.

explanation: Kepler's Second Law states that a line segment joining a planet and the Sun sweeps out equal areas during equal intervals of time. Therefore, to cover equal areas, a planet must travel faster when near the Sun (at perihelion) and slower when farther away (at aphelion).

text: 50. Kepler's Third Law of Planetary Motion states that the square of the orbital period ($T$) of a planet is directly proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis ($a$) of its orbit ($T^2 \propto a^3$). What does this law mathematically demonstrate?

options.text: Planets closer to the Sun take longer to complete one orbit.
Planets farther from the Sun have longer orbital periods and move at slower average orbital speeds.
All planets orbit the Sun in the exact same duration.

explanation: Kepler's Third Law shows that a planet's orbital period increases with its distance from the Sun. For example, Mercury takes only 88 days to orbit the Sun, while distant Neptune takes 165 years.

text: 51. In seismology, Primary waves (P-waves) are the fastest seismic waves generated during an earthquake. Which of the following is a key physical characteristic of P-waves?

options.text: They are transverse waves that can only pass through solid materials.
They are longitudinal (compressional) waves that can travel through solids, liquids, and gases.
They cause ground particles to vibrate perpendicular to the direction of wave propagation.
They are surface waves responsible for maximum structural damage.

explanation: P-waves are longitudinal waves (similar to sound waves) that compress and dilate the material they pass through. Because they are compressional, they can propagate through all states of matter: solids, liquids, and gases.

text: 52. Secondary waves (S-waves) are transverse shear waves that travel slower than P-waves. What critical physical property of S-waves allows geophysicists to prove the liquid state of Earth's Outer Core?

options.text: They increase in velocity when passing through liquids.
They can only propagate through solid media and cannot travel through liquids or gases.
They are completely reflected at the Mohorovicic discontinuity.
They travel in straight, unbent paths directly through the center of the Earth.

explanation: S-waves are transverse waves that require shear strength to propagate. Since liquids and gases have no shear strength, S-waves cannot travel through them. Their complete disappearance at the mantle-core boundary proved that Earth's outer core is liquid.

text: 53. Because of refraction and the liquid outer core, there are regions on Earth's surface where seismographs do not record direct seismic waves from an earthquake. What are the exact angular boundaries of the P-wave shadow zone relative to the epicenter?
explanation: The P-wave shadow zone occurs between 103° and 142° from the earthquake's epicenter. This band of missing waves is caused by the refraction of P-waves as they pass through the dense core.

text: 54. What are the exact angular boundaries of the S-wave shadow zone on Earth's surface relative to an earthquake's epicenter, and why is it larger than the P-wave shadow zone?

options.text: Between 103° and 142°; due to extreme refraction
From 103° to 180° (entire zone beyond 103°); because S-waves cannot propagate through the liquid outer core
Between 0° and 103°; because S-waves only travel along the equator
Between 120° and 160°; due to absorption by the inner core

explanation: The S-wave shadow zone is massive, extending continuously from 103° to 180° from the epicenter. This is because S-waves cannot pass through the liquid outer core, leaving more than 40% of the globe completely devoid of direct S-waves.

text: 55. Earth's interior is divided into layers separated by boundary zones called discontinuities. Which discontinuity separates Earth's continental/oceanic Crust from the underlying Mantle?
explanation: The Mohorovicic Discontinuity (commonly called the Moho) separates the Crust from the Mantle. It was discovered in 1909 by Croatian seismologist Andrija Mohorovicic who observed a sudden increase in seismic wave velocity at this boundary.

text: 56. Which discontinuity separates Earth's Mantle from the highly dense Outer Core?
explanation: The Gutenberg Discontinuity separates the lower Mantle from the Outer Core at a depth of approximately 2,900 km. It is marked by a sharp drop in P-wave velocity and the complete termination of S-waves.

text: 57. What is the correct order of Earth's seismic discontinuities from the surface down to the center of the Earth?
explanation: From surface to core, the correct order is: Conrad (upper/lower crust), Mohorovicic (crust/mantle), Repetti (upper/lower mantle), Gutenberg (mantle/outer core), and Lehmann (outer/solid inner core).

text: 58. In the structural composition of the Earth, the upper mantle contains a highly plastic, semi-fluid zone of partially molten rocks on which the lithospheric plates float. What is this layer called?
explanation: The Asthenosphere is the ductile, semi-fluid upper layer of the Earth's mantle, lying directly beneath the rigid lithosphere. It is the primary source of magma during volcanic eruptions.

text: 59. In physical geography, what is the term 'Sial' used to classify, and what are its two primary mineral constituents?

options.text: The oceanic crust, rich in Silica and Aluminium
The continental crust, rich in Silica and Aluminium
The Earth's core, rich in Silicon and Alums
The lower mantle, rich in Silver and Alloys

explanation: Sial represents the upper continental crust, dominated by lighter granite rocks rich in Silica ($Si$) and Aluminium ($Al$). The denser oceanic crust is called Sima, rich in Silica ($Si$) and Magnesium ($Ma$/$Mg$).

text: 60. The core of the Earth is also referred to as the 'Nife' layer in geochemistry. What does this acronym represent?
explanation: The term 'Nife' stands for Nickel ($Ni$) and Ferrum ($Fe$ - Iron), which are the two dominant metals that make up Earth's core, responsible for the planet's strong magnetic field.

text: 61. In navigation and cartography, what is a 'Great Circle' defined as, and what is its primary use in aviation?

options.text: Any circle parallel to the Equator, used to calculate local standard time zones.
A circle whose plane passes through the center of the Earth, representing the shortest distance between any two points on the globe.
A line of constant compass heading that cuts all meridians at the same angle.
An artificial boundary dividing the tropical and temperate zones.

explanation: A Great Circle is the largest possible circle that can be drawn on a sphere. Since its plane divides the sphere into two equal halves, the arc of a Great Circle represents the shortest flight path (geodesic) between two airports on Earth.

text: 62. What is a 'Rhumb Line' (or loxodromic curve) in navigation, and why was it traditionally favored by mariners despite being a longer path than a Great Circle?

options.text: It is the shortest path over the poles, bypassing wind resistance.
It is a line of constant bearing that cuts all meridians at the same angle, allowing sailors to steer a steady compass direction without changing course.
It is a curved path that follows the standard parallels of latitude.
It is a grid coordinate system used solely for mapping deep ocean floor ridges.

explanation: A Rhumb Line cuts all meridians of longitude at the same angle. Steering along a Rhumb Line allows a ship to maintain a constant compass heading, which is simple to navigate, even though it is not the shortest distance between two distant points.

text: 63. To establish standard times globally, the Earth is divided into 24 standard time zones. What is the standard longitudinal width of each of these time zones, corresponding to a 1-hour time difference?
explanation: Because the Earth rotates $360^\circ$ in 24 hours, dividing $360^\circ$ by 24 yields exactly $15^\circ$ per hour. Thus, each standard time zone spans $15^\circ$ of longitude.

text: 64. Due to vast territorial sizes and political boundaries, many countries have multiple time zones. Which country currently has the highest number of time zones, including its overseas territories?
explanation: France holds the record for the most time zones of any country, with 12 time zones, due to its numerous overseas departments and territories spread across the globe. Russia has 11 time zones, and the United States has 11.

text: 65. What is the term 'Van Allen Radiation Belts' used to define in space mechanics, and what protects Earth from their high-energy radiation?

options.text: Gaseous layers in the stratosphere; protected by the ozone layer
Zones of highly energetic charged particles trapped in Earth's magnetosphere, which is maintained by Earth's core dynamo
Rings of dust surrounding the asteroid belt; protected by Jupiter's gravity
Ice crystals in the mesosphere; protected by the greenhouse effect

explanation: The Van Allen Belts are two donut-shaped rings of highly energetic protons and electrons trapped by Earth's magnetic field (magnetosphere). Earth's magnetic field acts as a shield, deflecting harmful solar wind and cosmic radiation away from our atmosphere.

text: 66. In lunar mechanics, what is the difference between a Sidereal Month and a Synodic Month?

options.text: Sidereal is 29.5 days (phases cycle); Synodic is 27.3 days (orbit relative to stars)
Sidereal is 27.3 days (one orbit relative to distant stars); Synodic is 29.5 days (time to complete one full cycle of lunar phases)
Sidereal is the time between solstices; Synodic is the time between equinoxes
There is no physical difference; both terms are identical

explanation: A Sidereal Month is the time it takes the Moon to complete one full orbit around Earth relative to background stars (27.32 days). A Synodic Month is the time between consecutive New Moons (29.53 days), which is longer because Earth also moves along its orbit around the Sun during this time.

text: 67. Saturn's largest moon, Titan, is unique in our Solar System. What is the primary chemical composition of Titan's dense, opaque atmosphere?
explanation: Titan is the only known moon in the Solar System with a fully developed, dense atmosphere. It is composed of approximately 95% to 98% Nitrogen ($N_2$), along with traces of methane and other hydrocarbons.

text: 68. Neptune's largest moon, Triton, is historically noted for what unique orbital characteristic?

options.text: It is the only moon with active water geysers on its surface.
It orbits Neptune in a retrograde direction (opposite to the planet's rotation).
It has a perfectly circular orbit around the equator.
It was captured from the asteroid belt.

explanation: Triton is the only large moon in our Solar System that exhibits a retrograde orbit, orbiting Neptune in the opposite direction of the planet's rotation. This strongly indicates that Triton was captured from the Kuiper Belt.

text: 69. Mars has two tiny, irregular satellites, Phobos and Deimos. What is their geological origin, and which one is the smallest known moon in the Solar System?

options.text: Volcanic ejecta from Olympus Mons; Phobos is the smallest
Captured asteroids from the Asteroid Belt; Deimos is the smallest
Condensations of the early solar nebula; Deimos is the smallest
Debris from a proto-Earth collision; Phobos is the smallest

explanation: Both Phobos and Deimos are believed to be carbonaceous asteroids captured by Mars's gravity. Deimos, with a diameter of only ~12 km, is significantly smaller than Phobos (~22 km) and is one of the smallest known natural satellites.

text: 70. Uranus has a collection of natural satellites. Which of its moons is famous in planetary geomorphology for exhibiting a highly fractured, chaotic terrain that resembles a jigsaw puzzle?
explanation: Miranda has the most varied, bizarre, and fractured terrain of any body in the Solar System, showing deep canyons, scraped ridges, and massive fault scarps. This suggests it may have been shattered by a massive impact and reassembled by gravity.

text: 71. In astronomy, what is the 'Kuiper Belt' defined as, and which dwarf planet is its most famous resident?

options.text: A spherical shell of comets at the outer edge of the solar system; Halley's Comet
A disc-shaped region of icy bodies beyond the orbit of Neptune; Pluto
The ring system of Saturn; Titan
A cloud of hot plasma near the Sun's core; Ceres

explanation: The Kuiper Belt is a ring of icy bodies and dwarf planets extending from the orbit of Neptune (at ~30 AU) to about 50 AU from the Sun. Pluto is its most famous and largest known member.

text: 72. What is the 'Oort Cloud' in astrophysics, and how does it differ in structure and location from the Kuiper Belt?

options.text: It is a flat disc located between Mars and Jupiter.
It is an immense, spherical cloud of icy protoplanetary bodies believed to surround the Solar System at distances up to 100,000 AU, serving as the source of long-period comets.
It is a localized ring of dust near Uranus.
It is a magnetic belt around Earth.

explanation: Unlike the flat, disc-like Kuiper Belt, the Oort Cloud is a giant spherical shell that completely envelops our Solar System. It is located thousands of times farther out than the Kuiper Belt, serving as the reservoir for long-period comets.

text: 73. In the classification of space debris, what is the precise distinction between a Meteoroid, a Meteor, and a Meteorite?

options.text: Meteoroids are active comets, Meteors are dwarf planets, and Meteorites are asteroids.
A meteoroid is in space; a meteor is vaporizing in Earth's atmosphere ('shooting star'); and a meteorite is any surviving fragment that impacts Earth's surface.
Meteors are metallic, while Meteoroids are completely gaseous.
They represent the exact same object at different points in their 11-year solar cycle.

explanation: A Meteoroid is a small rock or metal fragment in space. When it enters Earth's atmosphere, frictional heating causes it to glow, creating a streak of light called a Meteor. If it survives the burn and lands on Earth's surface, it is called a Meteorite.

text: 74. In cartography and solar geometry, what is an 'Analemma' defined as?

options.text: The angle of Earth's magnetic tilt relative to its geographic axis
A figure-8 diagram showing the changing position of the Sun in the sky at a fixed time of day over the course of a year
The path followed by the Moon during a total lunar eclipse
The line of constant temperature on a global weather map

explanation: An Analemma is a figure-eight-shaped curve. It is plotted on globes and maps to show the Sun's declination and the equation of time throughout the year, caused by Earth's axial tilt and elliptical orbit.

text: 75. Due to the gravitational pull of the Moon and the Sun on Earth's equatorial bulge, Earth's axis undergoes a slow, continuous wobbling rotation. What is this phenomenon called, and how long does it take to complete one full cycle?
explanation: Axial Precession (Precession of the Equinoxes) is the slow, continuous wobble of Earth's rotational axis, which traces out a circle in space like a spinning top. One full cycle of precession takes approximately 25,800 years.

text: 76. Superimposed on Earth's long-term precession is a minor, short-period oscillation or 'nodding' of Earth's axis, primarily caused by the Moon's shifting orbital plane. What is this phenomenon called, and what is its cycle?
explanation: Nutation is a small, irregular 'nodding' motion of Earth's rotational axis. It has a principal period of 18.6 years, driven by variations in the gravitational pull of the Moon on Earth's equator.

text: 77. What is the 'Chandler Wobble' in geophysics, and what is its observed period?

options.text: A shift in Earth's orbital speed over 100 years
A small deviation in Earth's axis of rotation relative to its solid crust, with a period of about 433 days (14 months)
A change in the distance to the Moon every 28 days
The flip of Earth's magnetic poles every 200,000 years

explanation: The Chandler Wobble is a natural variation in the orientation of Earth's axis of rotation relative to the crust. It was discovered by astronomer Seth Carlo Chandler in 1891 and has an approximate period of 433 days.

text: 78. Milankovitch Cycles describe the collective effects of changes in Earth's movements on its climate over hundreds of thousands of years. What are the three primary orbital parameters that constitute these cycles?

options.text: Eccentricity (orbit shape), Obliquity (axial tilt), and Precession (axis wobble)

explanation: Milankovitch Cycles consist of: Eccentricity (variation in the shape of Earth's orbit from circular to elliptical; ~100,000-year cycle), Obliquity (changes in Earth's axial tilt from 22.1° to 24.5°; ~41,000-year cycle), and Precession (wobble of Earth's axis; ~23,000 to 26,000-year cycle). These drive ice ages.

text: 79. Due to gravitational interactions, the friction of ocean tides sliding across the shallow seabed acts as a brake on Earth's rotation. What is the long-term geodynamic consequence of this 'Tidal Friction'?

options.text: Earth's rotation speed is increasing, making days shorter.
Earth's rotation speed is gradually slowing down, causing the length of a day to increase by about 1.7 milliseconds per century.
Earth is moving closer to the Sun.
The Moon is moving closer to Earth.

explanation: Tidal Friction gradually slows Earth's rotation, transferring angular momentum to the Moon. As a result, Earth's day gets slightly longer (by ~1.7 to 2.3 milliseconds per century) and the Moon spirals slowly outward away from Earth at ~3.8 cm per year.

text: 80. In paleomagnetism, the study of iron-bearing minerals in volcanic rocks has proved that Earth's magnetic field is not static. What is this phenomenon of polarity swapping called?
explanation: Geomagnetic Reversals occur when Earth's magnetic North and South poles exchange positions. These reversals are preserved as alternating magnetic stripes in cooling seafloor basalt (sea-floor spreading), occurring irregularly every few hundred thousand years.
